Four Questions for the Nobel Prize API

Turning nested JSON into tidy data, and asking who the prize has moved toward

Author

Aniss Sahraoui

Published

November 8, 2026

library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)

snapshot <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/main/Week10B/data/"

accent   <- "#2a78d6"
accent_2 <- "#eb6834"
theme_nb <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot")

1 The API

The Nobel Prize Developer Zone publishes a public API that needs no key. I used the laureates endpoint, https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates, which returns one record per laureate with every prize that laureate has won nested inside it.

resp <- request("https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates") |>
  req_url_query(limit = 1) |>
  req_error(is_error = \(r) FALSE) |>
  req_perform()

parsed <- resp_body_json(resp)

tibble(
  status            = resp_status(resp),
  laureates_in_api  = parsed$meta$count,
  returned_this_call = length(parsed$laureates)
)
status laureates_in_api returned_this_call
200 1028 1

1.1 What one record looks like

A laureate is not a row. It is a deeply nested object: names repeat in up to three languages, birth sits inside its own object with a place inside that, and prizes arrive as an array because some laureates have won more than once.

one <- parsed$laureates[[1]]

tibble(
  field = c("knownName", "birth", "birth$place$country", "nobelPrizes", "affiliations"),
  shape = c(
    paste("object:", paste(names(one$knownName), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("object:", paste(names(one$birth), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("object:", paste(names(one$birth$place$country), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("array of", length(one$nobelPrizes), "prize object(s)"),
    paste("array inside each prize, with name / city / country objects")
  )
)
field shape
knownName object: en, se
birth object: date, year, place
birth\(place\)country object: en, no, se
nobelPrizes array of 1 prize object(s)
affiliations array inside each prize, with name / city / country objects

Three further wrinkles shape every decision below: organizations such as the Red Cross appear alongside people but carry orgName and founded instead of knownName and birth, with no gender; results are paginated, 100 at a time; and some birth dates record only a year, written as 1948-00-00.

2 Retrieving and Tidying the Data

The collection script pages through the whole list, flattens each record, and writes two tidy tables. The key part is the flattening:

# English label from a multi-language field, e.g. {en: "USA", se: "USA"}
en <- function(x) if (is.null(x)) NA_character_ else (x[["en"]] %||% NA_character_)

# First non-missing value. en() returns NA (not NULL) for an absent field and
# %||% only catches NULL, so organizations need a fallback that treats NA as
# "try the next one" — otherwise every organization loses its name.
first_present <- function(...) {
  vals <- c(...)
  vals <- vals[!is.na(vals)]
  if (length(vals)) vals[[1]] else NA_character_
}

laureates <- map_dfr(laureates_raw, \(l) tibble(
  laureate_id     = l$id,
  name            = first_present(en(l$knownName), en(l$orgName)),
  is_organization = !is.null(l$orgName),
  gender          = l$gender %||% NA_character_,
  birth_date      = first_present(l$birth$date %||% NA_character_,
                                  l$founded$date %||% NA_character_),
  birth_country_now = first_present(en(l$birth$place$countryNow),
                                    en(l$founded$place$countryNow)),
  n_prizes        = length(l$nobelPrizes)
))

# One row per laureate per prize: a two-time winner becomes two rows.
prizes <- map_dfr(laureates_raw, \(l) {
  map_dfr(l$nobelPrizes, \(p) {
    aff <- if (length(p$affiliations)) p$affiliations[[1]] else NULL
    tibble(
      laureate_id             = l$id,
      award_year              = as.integer(p$awardYear),
      category                = en(p$category),
      prize_status            = p$prizeStatus %||% NA_character_,
      affiliation_country_now = if (is.null(aff)) NA_character_ else en(aff$countryNow)
    )
  })
})

The full script is fetch_nobel.R. Its output is saved to CSV so this report renders from a fixed snapshot rather than a live call.

laureates <- read_csv(paste0(snapshot, "nobel_laureates.csv"),
                      col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  mutate(is_organization = as.logical(is_organization),
         n_prizes        = as.integer(n_prizes),
         # Year only: 48 birth dates are recorded as e.g. 1948-00-00, so the
         # year is reliable but the exact date is not.
         birth_year      = as.integer(str_sub(birth_date, 1, 4)))

prizes <- read_csv(paste0(snapshot, "nobel_prizes.csv"),
                   col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  mutate(award_year = as.integer(award_year))

# One row per laureate-prize, with the laureate's own details attached.
awards <- prizes |>
  left_join(
    laureates |> select(laureate_id, is_organization, gender, birth_year,
                        birth_country, birth_country_now),
    by = "laureate_id"
  )

tibble(
  laureate_records   = nrow(laureates),
  laureate_prize_rows = nrow(awards),
  repeat_winners     = sum(laureates$n_prizes > 1),
  organizations      = sum(laureates$is_organization),
  years_covered      = paste(min(awards$award_year), "-", max(awards$award_year))
)
laureate_records laureate_prize_rows repeat_winners organizations years_covered
1028 1036 7 28 1901 - 2026

Seven laureates have won more than once, producing the eight extra prize rows:

laureates |>
  filter(n_prizes > 1) |>
  select(name, is_organization, n_prizes) |>
  arrange(desc(n_prizes))
name is_organization n_prizes
International Committee of the Red Cross TRUE 3
Frederick Sanger FALSE 2
John Bardeen FALSE 2
K. Barry Sharpless FALSE 2
Linus Pauling FALSE 2
Marie Curie FALSE 2
Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees TRUE 2

2.1 Cleaning decisions

bind_rows(
  laureates |> summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing") |>
    mutate(table = "laureates"),
  prizes |> summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing") |>
    mutate(table = "prizes")
) |>
  filter(missing > 0) |>
  select(table, column, missing)
table column missing
laureates gender 28
laureates birth_date 1
laureates birth_country 7
laureates birth_country_now 7
laureates birth_continent 31
laureates death_date 331
laureates birth_year 1
prizes affiliation_name 270
prizes affiliation_country 273
prizes affiliation_country_now 273

Each gap is kept rather than patched, with a reason:

  • gender is missing for all 28 organizations. They are excluded from the gender question rather than counted as unknown.
  • affiliation_country is missing for 273 prizes. Peace and Literature laureates usually have no institutional affiliation. These are excluded from Question 4, which needs both countries, and the report states how many rows that leaves.
  • death_date is missing for 331 laureates, who are living. That is information, not absence.
  • Country names are taken from countryNow rather than country. The raw field records the country as it was named at the time, so Marie Curie’s birthplace is “Russian Empire” while countryNow says “Poland”. Using present-day names makes countries comparable across 125 years.
prizes |> count(prize_status)
prize_status n
declined 2
received 1033
restricted 1

Two prizes were declined and one is restricted. They stay in the counts, because the prize was still awarded.

3 Question 1: How has the number of laureates changed over time?

The question. The prize has grown from a handful of awards a year to a crowded field. Counting by decade and category shows when that happened.

by_decade <- awards |>
  mutate(decade = 10 * (award_year %/% 10)) |>
  count(decade, category)

by_decade |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(laureates = sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Decade", "Laureates"))
Decade Laureates
1900 57
1910 40
1920 54
1930 56
1940 43
1950 72
1960 79
1970 104
1980 97
1990 104
2000 123
2010 121
2020 86 
by_decade |>
  mutate(category = fct_reorder(category, n, sum, .desc = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = n, fill = category)) +
  geom_col(width = 8) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Laureates per decade, by category",
       x = NULL, y = "Laureates") +
  theme_nb +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

The answer. Numbers roughly doubled: the 1900s produced 57 laureates and the 2000s produced 123. The cause is sharing rather than more prizes — a single prize is now routinely split between two or three people, where early prizes usually went to one. Economic Sciences only begins in 1969, which is visible as the category appearing part-way along.

4 Question 2: How has the share of women changed?

The question. Women are a small minority of laureates. Is that changing, and does it differ by category?

people <- awards |> filter(!is_organization)

people |>
  count(gender) |>
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Gender", "Prizes", "%"))
Gender Prizes %
female 70 7
male 935 93 
people |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(
    prizes      = n(),
    women       = sum(gender == "female"),
    pct_women   = round(100 * sum(gender == "female") / n(), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_women)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Prizes", "Women", "% women"))
Category Prizes Women % women
Peace 113 21 18.6
Literature 123 19 15.4
Physiology or Medicine 235 14 6.0
Chemistry 202 8 4.0
Economic Sciences 101 3 3.0
Physics 231 5 2.2 
people |>
  mutate(decade = 10 * (award_year %/% 10)) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(pct_women = 100 * sum(gender == "female") / n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = pct_women)) +
  geom_col(fill = accent, width = 8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct_women)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "The share of women has risen, from a very low base",
       x = NULL, y = "% of prizes to women") +
  theme_nb

The answer. The share has risen from 5.4% in the 1900s to 19.5% in the 2020s, with the 1950s recording none at all. The gap between categories is wider than the change over time: Peace sits at 18.6% and Literature at 15.4%, while Physics is at 2.2% — five women in 231 prizes.

5 Question 3: How old are laureates when they win?

The question. The prize is often awarded long after the work it recognises. Age at the time of the award makes that lag visible, and shows whether it is growing.

ages <- people |>
  filter(!is.na(birth_year)) |>
  mutate(age = award_year - birth_year)

tibble(
  prizes_with_age = nrow(ages),
  mean_age        = round(mean(ages$age), 1),
  median_age      = median(ages$age),
  youngest        = min(ages$age),
  oldest          = max(ages$age)
)
prizes_with_age mean_age median_age youngest oldest
1005 60.6 61 17 97

Age here is award year minus birth year, not an exact age in years. That is a deliberate simplification: 48 birth dates record only a year, so a precise calculation would silently drop them. The approximation is at most a year out.

ages |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(prizes = n(), mean_age = round(mean(age), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(mean_age) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Prizes", "Mean age"))
Category Prizes Mean age
Physics 231 57.8
Physiology or Medicine 235 59.0
Chemistry 202 59.5
Peace 113 61.0
Literature 123 65.0
Economic Sciences 101 67.2 
ggplot(ages, aes(x = award_year, y = age)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.4, color = accent) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = accent_2, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Laureates are winning later in life",
       x = "Award year", y = "Age at award") +
  theme_nb
bind_rows(
  ages |> slice_min(age, n = 3) |> mutate(group = "Youngest"),
  ages |> slice_max(age, n = 3) |> mutate(group = "Oldest")
) |>
  select(group, name, category, award_year, age) |>
  kable(col.names = c("", "Name", "Category", "Year", "Age"))
Name Category Year Age
Youngest Malala Yousafzai Peace 2014 17
Youngest Lawrence Bragg Physics 1915 25
Youngest Nadia Murad Peace 2018 25
Oldest John B. Goodenough Chemistry 2019 97
Oldest Arthur Ashkin Physics 2018 96
Oldest Henri B. Kagan Chemistry 2026 96

The answer. The mean is 60.6 and the median 61, but the trend is the real finding: laureates awarded before 1970 averaged 55.2, and those since average 64.0 — nearly nine years older. Economic Sciences has the oldest laureates at 67.2 and Physics the youngest at 57.8. The range runs from Malala Yousafzai at 17 to John B. Goodenough at 97.

6 Question 4: Which countries lost laureates, and which gained them?

The question. This one needs two fields compared rather than counted. Each prize record holds the laureate’s country of birth and the country of the institution they were working at when they won. Where those differ, a country educated someone whose prize was credited elsewhere.

movers <- awards |>
  filter(
    !is_organization,                      # organizations have no birthplace
    !is.na(birth_country_now),             # both countries must be known
    !is.na(affiliation_country_now)
  ) |>
  mutate(moved = birth_country_now != affiliation_country_now)

tibble(
  all_prize_rows      = nrow(awards),
  organizations       = sum(awards$is_organization),
  no_affiliation      = sum(is.na(awards$affiliation_country_now)),
  usable_for_question = nrow(movers),
  moved               = sum(movers$moved),
  pct_moved           = round(100 * mean(movers$moved), 1)
)
all_prize_rows organizations no_affiliation usable_for_question moved pct_moved
1036 31 273 761 244 32.1

Only 761 of 1036 prize rows can answer this, because Peace and Literature laureates usually have no listed institution. The result describes the laureates who worked at universities and laboratories, which is most of the science prizes.

lost   <- movers |> filter(moved) |> count(country = birth_country_now,       name = "lost")
gained <- movers |> filter(moved) |> count(country = affiliation_country_now, name = "gained")

net_flow <- full_join(lost, gained, by = "country") |>
  replace_na(list(lost = 0, gained = 0)) |>
  mutate(net = gained - lost)

bind_rows(
  net_flow |> slice_max(net, n = 5) |> mutate(group = "Biggest net gainers"),
  net_flow |> slice_min(net, n = 5) |> mutate(group = "Biggest net losers")
) |>
  select(group, country, lost, gained, net) |>
  kable(col.names = c("", "Country", "Laureates lost", "Laureates gained", "Net"))
Country Laureates lost Laureates gained Net
Biggest net gainers USA 4 134 130
Biggest net gainers United Kingdom 24 35 11
Biggest net gainers Switzerland 3 12 9
Biggest net gainers Denmark 0 2 2
Biggest net gainers Germany 24 25 1
Biggest net gainers Sweden 3 4 1
Biggest net losers Poland 19 0 -19
Biggest net losers Canada 15 6 -9
Biggest net losers Scotland 9 0 -9
Biggest net losers Austria 10 2 -8
Biggest net losers Hungary 8 0 -8
Biggest net losers Russia 11 3 -8
Biggest net losers the Netherlands 9 1 -8 
net_flow |>
  filter(abs(net) >= 4) |>
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, net),
         direction = if_else(net > 0, "Net gain", "Net loss")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = net, y = country, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = net), hjust = ifelse(net_flow |> filter(abs(net) >= 4) |> pull(net) > 0, -0.3, 1.3),
            size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Net gain" = accent, "Net loss" = accent_2), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) +
  labs(title = "One country gains; everyone else loses",
       x = "Laureates gained minus laureates lost", y = NULL) +
  theme_nb +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
movers |>
  filter(moved) |>
  count(birth_country_now, affiliation_country_now, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Born in", "Awarded while working in", "Laureates"))
Born in Awarded while working in Laureates
United Kingdom USA 19
Canada USA 15
Germany USA 11
Poland Germany 9
France USA 8
Japan USA 7
Scotland United Kingdom 7
China USA 6 
movers |>
  summarise(
    born_in_usa      = sum(birth_country_now == "USA"),
    affiliated_usa   = sum(affiliation_country_now == "USA"),
    prizes           = n()
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_born = round(100 * born_in_usa / prizes, 1),
         pct_affiliated = round(100 * affiliated_usa / prizes, 1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Born in USA", "Working in USA", "Prizes", "% born", "% working"))
Born in USA Working in USA Prizes % born % working
272 402 761 35.7 52.8

The answer. Just under a third of these prizes, 32.1%, went to someone working outside their country of birth, and the flow is overwhelmingly in one direction. The United States has a net gain of 130 laureates, losing only 4 while gaining 134. No other country comes close: the United Kingdom is next at +11, and Switzerland at +9.

The largest losers are Poland (−19), then Canada, Scotland, Austria, Hungary, Russia and the Netherlands. The single biggest flow is United Kingdom to USA, 19 laureates, followed by Canada to USA at 15 and Germany to USA at 11.

The clearest way to see it: 35.7% of these laureates were born in the United States, but 52.8% were working there when they won.

movers |>
  mutate(decade = 10 * (award_year %/% 10)) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(prizes = n(), n_moved = sum(moved),
            pct_moved = round(100 * sum(moved) / n(), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Decade", "Prizes", "Moved", "% moved"))
Decade Prizes Moved % moved
1900 33 14 42.4
1910 24 7 29.2
1920 33 9 27.3
1930 39 9 23.1
1940 30 11 36.7
1950 55 18 32.7
1960 60 17 28.3
1970 78 25 32.1
1980 76 27 35.5
1990 75 25 33.3
2000 97 26 26.8
2010 94 32 34.0
2020 67 24 35.8

Interestingly, the share who moved has not risen much: it was 42% in the 1900s and 36% in the 2020s, hovering around a third throughout. What changed is the destination. The early movements were largely within Europe — Poland to Germany is the fourth-largest flow in the whole dataset — while the modern ones nearly all end in the United States.

7 Conclusions

  • The prize has roughly doubled in size, from 57 laureates in the 1900s to 123 in the 2000s, mostly because prizes are now shared between two or three people.
  • Women have gone from 5.4% of laureates to 19.5%, but the category gap is larger than the change over time: Peace is at 18.6% and Physics at 2.2%.
  • Laureates are winning almost nine years later in life than before 1970, 64.0 against 55.2, which suggests a lengthening gap between the work and its recognition.
  • The United States has gained 130 laureates it did not produce, while Poland has lost 19. A third of scientific laureates were working outside their country of birth when they won, and that share has been roughly constant for a century — only the destination has changed.

What the data cannot say. Question 4 rests on 761 of 1,036 prize rows, because Peace and Literature laureates rarely list an institution, so it is really a finding about the sciences. The affiliation is also only the one recorded at the time of the award: a laureate who was born in Germany, trained in the UK and won in the USA appears here simply as Germany to USA.

8 Source

Nobel Prize API v2.1, laureates endpoint, https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates. Data from nobelprize.org, used under the Nobel Prize API terms of use.
